title: Shell Tools and Environment
lead: Make the shell work for you: history, completion, shortcuts, quoting, variables, PATH, wildcards and command substitution.
objectives: You reuse old commands with history, !! and Ctrl+R.
You work fast with Tab completion and the Ctrl+C/L/A/E shortcuts.
You know the difference between double quotes, single quotes and the backslash.
You define variables, pass them on with export, and read and extend PATH.
You shorten commands with wildcards (*, ?, []), brace expansion and $().

sections.title: Command history
body: The shell remembers what you type. `history` shows a numbered list; `history 5` shows only the last 5 commands. The Up arrow (↑) recalls the previous command.

`!!` runs the previous command again. Its most common use is `sudo !!`, which adds the `sudo` you forgot. `Ctrl+R` **searches** the history: type a few letters, the matching old command appears, press Enter to run it.

commands.what: Lists the commands you ran, with numbers.
commands.where: When you want to recall a long command from yesterday.
commands.why: Saves retyping and shows what you did.

commands.what: Shows only the last 5 commands.
commands.where: When a short overview is enough.
commands.why: You don't drown in a long list.

commands.what: Runs the previous command again, unchanged.
commands.why: No need to retype the same command.

commands.what: Searches backwards through the history.
commands.where: Finding a very old, long command.
commands.why: Much faster than scrolling with the arrow key.

sections.tip: After pressing Ctrl+R, press Ctrl+R again to jump to the next older match.

sections.title: Tab completion and shortcuts
body: The `Tab` key completes command, file and folder names. With one match it completes; with several, press Tab twice to list the options. It saves time and prevents typos.

A few shortcuts cover half of daily work: `Ctrl+C` stops a running command, `Ctrl+L` clears the screen (same as `clear`), `Ctrl+A` jumps to the start of the line, `Ctrl+E` to the end. With `alias` you can give long commands a short name.

commands.what: Completes the name you typed or lists the options.
Interrupts the running command (sends SIGINT).
commands.where: A command that hangs or never ends.
commands.why: You leave the command without closing the terminal.

commands.what: Moves the cursor to the start / end of the line.
commands.why: Faster than stepping with the arrow keys.

commands.what: Clears the screen; Ctrl+L does the same.
Gives a command a short alias.
commands.why: Less typing. To make it permanent, put it in `~/.bashrc`.

sections.tip: Never type a long file name by hand; type the first letters and press Tab.

sections.title: Quotes and escaping
body: Before running a command the shell interprets special characters. Quotes control that. Inside **double quotes** `$variable` and `$(command)` are expanded. Inside **single quotes** everything stays literal. A **backslash** (`\`) removes the special meaning of one character.
File names with spaces also need quotes: `cat "my notes.txt"`. Without quotes the shell sees two separate arguments.

commands.what: Double quotes: variables expand, spaces are kept.
Single quotes: nothing expands, text is printed literally.
Removes the special meaning of the next character.

sections.tip: When in doubt, put variables in double quotes: `"$FILE"` also works with names containing spaces.

sections.title: Variables and export
body: Define a variable with `NAME=alice`; **no spaces around the equals sign**. Read it with `$NAME`. A variable defined this way lives only in this shell.

To let programs you start see it, use `export NAME=alice`. `env` shows all exported **environment variables** (`HOME`, `USER`, `PATH`, `SHELL`...). Changes made with `export` are lost when the terminal closes; to keep them, write them into `~/.bashrc`.

commands.what: Defines a shell variable (no spaces).
commands.why: You don't retype the same value.

commands.what: Prints the value of the variable.
Passes the variable on to child programs.
commands.why: Without export the variable stays in this shell only.

commands.what: Lists environment variables.
Removes a variable.
commands.where: Dropping a variable you no longer need.

sections.tip: Don't write `NAME = alice` (with spaces): the shell looks for a command called `NAME` and fails.

sections.title: PATH: where commands are found
body: When you type a command, the shell searches the folders in the `PATH` variable in order. Folders are separated by `:`. `which ls` shows the path found, `type ls` shows the kind of command (program, builtin).
To add a folder with your own tools, append it to `PATH`. Keep the old value: `export PATH=$PATH:~/bin`. If you only write `PATH=~/bin`, even `ls` can no longer be found.

commands.what: Shows the search folders.
commands.where: First place to look on 'command not found'.
commands.why: You see why a command isn't found.

commands.what: Shows the full path of a command.
commands.why: Avoids mixing up programs with the same name.

commands.what: Tells whether a command is a program or a builtin.
Adds `~/bin` to the search path.
commands.where: Calling your own scripts by name.
commands.why: No need to type the full path each time.

sections.warn: Never assign something like `PATH=/new/dir` that throws away the old value; no command, `ls` included, will be found. Close and reopen the terminal to recover.
sections.tip: To make it permanent, add the same `export` line to `~/.bashrc`.

sections.title: Wildcards (globbing)
body: The **shell** expands wildcards, not the command. `*` matches anything (including nothing), `?` exactly one character, `[abc]` one of the characters in brackets. For `ls *.txt` the shell first turns the pattern into file names, then hands them to `ls`.
If nothing matches, the shell leaves the pattern as it is. Before delete commands, test the pattern with `echo`: `echo *.log`.

commands.what: Any sequence of characters.
commands.where: Selecting files of the same type.

commands.what: Exactly one character.
One of the characters in brackets.

sections.warn: `rm *` deletes every file in the current folder. First check what matches with `echo *`, then run `rm`.
sections.tip: Hidden files (starting with `.`) are not matched by `*`.

sections.title: Brace expansion and command substitution
body: Brace expansion generates text: `file{1,2,3}.txt` becomes three names, `f{1..3}` becomes `f1 f2 f3`. The files don't have to exist, which makes it ideal for bulk `touch` and `mkdir`.
`$(command)` runs the command and substitutes its **output**: `echo "Today: $(date)"`. You can also store output in a variable: `USERNAME=$(whoami)`.

commands.what: Multiplies a comma-separated list.
Generates a number or letter range.
Puts a command's output inside another command.
commands.where: Dynamic values like date, user, host name.
commands.why: You use the live value instead of hard-coding it.

sections.tip: The old `` `command` `` form works too, but `$()` is far more readable when nested.

sections.title: echo, printf and exit code
body: `echo` prints text and variables. For formatted output use `printf`: `%s` is text, `%d` a number, `\n` a newline. `printf` adds no newline automatically.
Every command leaves an **exit code**: `0` means success, anything else an error. Read the last one with `$?`. In scripts this is how you check for success.

commands.what: Prints text or a variable's value.
Produces formatted output.
commands.where: Aligned output or exact control over newlines.

commands.what: Prints the exit code of the last command.
commands.why: `0` is success, non-zero is an error.

vm.intro: Run the commands below on your own VM (Ubuntu, Rocky, Alma or WSL). The commands in this module are harmless; still, extend `PATH` with `export` and never overwrite it with `PATH=`.

v01.title: Explore the history
v01.text: Run a few commands, then show the last lines of the history. Then try `!!` and `Ctrl+R`.

blocks.cmd:
echo one
echo two
history | tail -n 5
blocks.expected:
101  echo one
  102  echo two
  103  history | tail -n 5

blocks.cmd:
# Press Ctrl+R, type 'echo', press Enter; then:
!!

differs: The numbers will differ with your history; the order of the lines matters.
If `!!` doesn't work, make sure you are in Bash: `echo $SHELL`.

v02.title: Variable and export
v02.text: Define a variable, export it, and check whether a child shell can see it.

blocks.cmd:
MYVAR=hello
bash -c 'echo "child: [$MYVAR]"'
export MYVAR
bash -c 'echo "child: [$MYVAR]"'
env | grep MYVAR

differs: If the first line isn't `child: []`, `MYVAR` was exported earlier; reopen the terminal.
Copy all three lines when pasting the output.

v03.title: Quote difference
v03.text: Print the same text with double and single quotes and see the difference.
differs: If your user isn't `student`, your own name appears; that is normal.

v04.title: Wildcards and braces
v04.text: In a safe folder, create files with braces and match them with wildcards.
differs: If your home isn't `/home/student`, the path looks different; the file names must be the same.
In `WSL`, `~` is your Linux home, not the Windows side.

v05.title: Add your own tool to PATH
v05.text: Write a tiny script, add its folder to `PATH` and call it by name.

blocks.cmd:
mkdir -p ~/tools
printf '#!/bin/bash\necho tool works\n' > ~/tools/hello
chmod +x ~/tools/hello
export PATH=$PATH:~/tools
hello
which hello

differs: On `command not found`, check with `echo $PATH` that the `tools` path was added.

v06.title: Try the shortcuts
v06.text: Type `sleep 100` and stop it with `Ctrl+C`. Then type a long command and move around with `Ctrl+A` and `Ctrl+E`, clear the screen with `Ctrl+L`. Type `~/Doc` and complete it with Tab. When finished, press "Done".
differs: If your terminal emulator grabs Ctrl+L, type `clear` instead.
If Tab does nothing, press it twice; with several matches they are listed.

q1.explain: `!!` is replaced by the previous command; `sudo !!` is very common.

q2.explain: Variables are not expanded inside single quotes; the text is printed as is.

q3.q: Which command makes a variable visible to child programs?
q3.explain: `export` puts the variable into the environment; `env` then shows it.

q4.q: What is the output of `echo f{1..3}`?
q4.explain: The shell performs brace expansion and produces three separate words.

summary: `Tab` completes; `Ctrl+C` interrupts, `Ctrl+L` clears, `Ctrl+A/E` move within the line.
`$` expands in double quotes, not in single quotes, and `\` protects one character.
`NAME=value` has no spaces; child programs need `export`.
`PATH` holds the folders searched for commands; extend it with `export PATH=$PATH:...`.
`*`, `?`, `[]` are wildcards; `{a,b}` is brace expansion; `$()` substitutes command output.

glossary.meaning: The list of commands the shell remembers.
A variable carrying settings for the shell and child programs (HOME, PATH, USER).
A `:`-separated list of folders searched for commands.
Expansion of `*`, `?`, `[]` patterns into file names.
The number a command leaves behind; `0` is success, anything else an error.
